title: How to Find and Commission Local Artists in Berlin | Countercult
description: A practical guide for Berlin agencies, brands, and cultural teams to find artists through public profiles, local context, direct conversation, consent, and paid terms.
heading: How to find local artists in Berlin

intro.text: If you are searching for local artists in Berlin, the first useful question is not who is most visible online. It is what the project needs, who should be involved, and whether the artist wants the work. This guide is for agencies, brands, and cultural teams that want to find and commission artists without turning the city into a contact list.

paragraphs.text: Set out the purpose, audience, place, dates, decision-maker, and budget before approaching artists. Separate the artist fee from travel, materials, access, production, and usage costs. For a Berlin brief, name the district or venue, audience, working language, dates, and production or access needs. Berlin alone is not a brief.

Start with artists’ own websites, public portfolios, artist-run spaces, exhibitions, open studios, neighbourhood programmes, and independent publishers. Countercult’s public Network includes artists and cultural workers who chose to publish a profile. Browse by city, practice, and tag in the
. A public profile is an invitation to learn about the work, not automatic permission to use images or assume availability.

Some of the most relevant creative talent will not appear in a standard agency list. Read the artist’s work and local context, then ask whether the person is open to the specific project. Do not treat search visibility, social reach, or a city tag as proof of fit.

State the fee, scope, timeline, expenses, production support, credit, rights, and payment schedule in writing. Pay for the work and for any agreed use of it. Exposure is not a substitute for a fee, and a commission should not quietly expand beyond its original scope.

Give the artist a real choice about whether to participate and how the work is described. Agree how the finished project can be documented, credited, and shared. Ask for a referral only if the artist is comfortable making one.

The Berlin Senate's cultural policy overview cites more than 160,000 employees in the city's cultural and creative economy. This is a sector-wide figure, not a count of artists available for commission. It shows the scale of the wider ecosystem and why a careful, brief-led search is more useful than treating Berlin as one talent list.
